chapter: War years, Decca records and La Conga
title: Jack Robbins's file of rejected Latin numbers
summary: The tunes recorded were Robbins stock numbers marked no good by Latin bandleaders; Mario's arrangements made them hits.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: I see. All right. I noticed that your twenty-six recordings with Miguelito Valdes and the Machito orchestra, you had a lot of good numbers. Did you have to go looking for these numbers? Did you have to ask for composers to give you these numbers or did they just come up to you and offered them?
No, no, those particular numbers they was published by Robbins.
Those were stock numbers?
Yes, they were numbers that he had for a long time but he never touched it until Miguelito came to the United States.
"Eco", "Tabu", "Enoro", all those numbers?
All those numbers. Those numbers they were published by Jack Robbins before Miguelito came to the United States.
My goodness!! Wow!!

All those numbers that was in files with the note: no good - fair - could be good if it change; because there was a lot of new composers that were jealous about the Cuban composers because they were Cuban and Puerto Rican
that were living in the United States, so they want to stop all those numbers coming from Cuba to be recorded here.
All right. Who was making the decision whether they were good numbers or not?
Oh, I don't want to call the names because ahh-
Are they well-known names ......
Oh yeah, big names.
...... musicians?
Musicians, band leaders.
Band leaders. Could we now ehh go a little further, give a hint? Would it be ahh a pianist or a trumpeter or a vocalist?
No, most of them they were pianist.
I see. Okay, I get you now. All right. Tunes like 'Tanga-Si'....... (End of cassette 2, side 1)
He never was involved with a Latin thing. He left that to the Latin fellow to say if the number was good or not good.
I see.
Musically, he knows that it was good, but they claimed that the lyrics that they wouldn't understand in South America or in Puerto Rico or in Santo Domingo.

Okay, let me try to clear this a little clearer. In other words, it was up to a Latin band leader who was a pianist at the time, to decide whether these numbers were good; but he must have been a top band leader at the same time for them to turn......
Definetely.
.....he didn't want any competition. Okay, I see, I get the picture. All right, so how did Marcelino Guerra finally break all that up? Was it you and Mario that ......
Because Mario took all those numbers and we ...
He made arrangements.

We made arrangements and play over the radio; and Jack Robbins flipped and everybody just applauded, crazy, they went crazy about the number, so Jack Robbins said: "Gee, but how come"? "These numbers, they was no good." And then I like them, I said: I am a Latin, I like the numbers, and Diosa Costelo, Pupi Campo, all those numbers that became popular to practically all the new band leaders. That was the Pupi Campo repertoire and practically everyone was copying.
I see. So, about how long did those numbers stay in that file unnoticed?
Could be four, five years.
